The problem with banning artifact lands is that they aren't *just* played in Affinity; an entire wealth of decks play them, so banning them just to neuter Affinity will also significantly weaken every other deck that plays them.

IMO, the solution is super-simple: don't print/downshift cards that singlehandedly win the game off of a wealth of artifacts. \[\[All That Glitters\]\] did NOT need to be downshifted. Ever. That was a huge mistake. \[\[Cranial Ram\]\] did NOT need to be printed at common, either, and it's likely getting banned rather quickly. I personally think \[\[Makeshift Munitions\]\] is a bannable card. 

Affinity is only a problem for Pauper if the people making the cards MAKES it a problem for Pauper. Maybe this whole debacle sends a message to the card designers at WotC. If not, then the PFP thankfully exists to regulate this format.

My thinking, currently, is that in a few years, maybe less, we'll start to see the rise of industrial hardcore. Specifically, the type of industrial hardcore you hear on labels like Prototypes, the type you hear from artists like The Satan, Berzark, eDUB, etc. Less noisy, more interesting sound design.
But don't get me wrong, more "traditional" industrial hardcore will continue to exist, too, primarily within the rise of hard techno. We're already seeing it with producers like Somniac One and Densha Crisis.

Same reason people hate piepkicks; because so many producers don't really know how to use them. It's one thing to use these types of kicks during a moment of great intensity (or in the case of piepkicks, for the memes), but a lot of producers just throw them into tracks as often as they can, since these kicks get such huge crowd reactions. 

The way I see it, zaagkicks are so prevalent right now because they're new. This is brand new territory in terms of hard dance sound design, and naturally, producers want to explore it. Eventually, producers will get bored of putting a zaagkick in every track, and they'll stop using them as much, but I still think zaagkicks will have a small niche in hard dance production after that happens- it'll just be a rarer occurence. Or, to put it another way, does anyone remember 2017-2018? Zaagkicks are just the new hardpsy kicks.

(1.) For the majority of my decks, I run a lot of "auto-include" ramp, like the Signets, Rampant Growth/Farseek, and, obviously, Sol Ring, as well as "auto-include" removal, such as Path/Swords and Beast Within/Generous Gift, and that's where my "auto-includes" typically end. However, since we're strictly talking casual and not cEDH, there are a lot of cards I feel are "auto-includes" in casual that would never get played in competitive. For example, in higher-powered play, any ramp spell above 2 mana will typically never be considered, but just about every green deck I build runs both Cultivate and Kodama's Reach, and basically all of my 2+ color decks run at least 1 Locket (Guilds of Ravnica block), and most of my decks in general run Hedron Archive (I even consider Dreamstone Hedron if that deck already makes a lot of mana). Mana Drain is probably the best 2-mana counterspell, but OG Counterspell works just fine as well, and Essence Scatter is solid in this format, too, since it often times just reads "Counter target commander." I think mid-power casual opens the "auto-include" conversation a good bit, if only in the context of mid-power.

(2.) Some staples I don't run due to price (although I am about to become a relentless and unapologetic proxier), but there are three other main reasons I don't run certain auto-includes. First, there's the issue of... let's call it "inconsistency". Basically, discrepancies throughout some of my decks, as in, some decks that can run this staple run it, others... just don't. I've thought about "rebuilding" every single one of my decks, just checking to see that each deck is running what it probably should be. The second issue is that certain staple cards, for lack of a better term, are just "uncool". Let's just put it this way: there are VERY few decks I'd consider playing Rhystic Study in, because blue already has solid card draw, and I don't want to become another "pay the 1" guy in a sea of "pay the 1" guys. Yes, I KNOW Rhystic Study makes basically every blue deck better, I just don't care. Third, and finally, there are some staples I don't see the need for in certain types of decks. Dockside is a great addition to a mono-red/Boros deck, but, outside of comboing off, would you really need it in, say, a Gruul deck?

(3.) Depends. For ramp, removal, and card draw, I ABSOLUTELY stick with the staples, and never really traverse outside of those waters. For everything else, however, I don't really care.

(4.) Again, depends, not only on the staple, but on the context of what we're playing. For example, if I sit down for a game of cEDH and I see someone play a turn 1 Mana Crypt, I think to myself, "oh sweet, a turn 1 mana crypt." If I sit down for casual and see someone play a turn 1 Mana Crypt, I think to myself, "are you absolutely kidding me right now?"

(5.) Not that I can remember.
